market_context: United States; USDA composition for firm tofu and cooked chicken breast
title: Tofu vs Chicken: A Nutrition Comparison

seo.title: Tofu vs Chicken: Protein, Calories, Fat and Nutrients
seo.meta_description: Chicken breast has much more protein per 100 g; tofu adds fiber, unsaturated fat and can provide substantial calcium depending on the coagulant.
seo.search_intent: Compare firm tofu and chicken breast using realistic amounts and explain why they are not nutritionally identical substitutes.

excerpt: Cooked chicken breast is much more protein-dense, at about 31 grams per 100 grams versus roughly 15–18 grams in firm tofu. Tofu, however, provides unsaturated fat, some fiber and can be a substantial calcium source when made with calcium sulfate. They can fill the same place on a plate without being gram-for-gram equivalents.
content_html:
Tofu and chicken can occupy exactly the same center-of-the-plate role, but that does not make them nutritionally interchangeable. Chicken breast packs almost twice as much protein into the same weight; tofu provides less protein but adds plant fat, some fiber and minerals that vary substantially by product.

If you want the most protein for relatively few calories, chicken has the advantage. If you want a plant protein that also brings unsaturated fat, fiber and sometimes a lot of calcium, tofu is doing a different job.

Per 100 grams, the protein gap is large

Firm tofuCooked chicken breast
Calories~130–150~165
Protein~15–18 g~31 g
Fat~8–9 g~3.6 g
Fiber~1–2 g0 g

The interesting part is that calories are fairly close while protein is not. Tofu contains substantially more fat, while skinless chicken breast is extremely lean.

Per-100-gram numbers measure concentration, not the serving you are required to eat. A plant-based meal can simply use a larger tofu portion or combine tofu with other protein foods rather than expecting the two foods to match gram for gram.

A normal serving shows what that difference means

About 5 ounces of firm tofu provide roughly 21–25 grams of protein. Five ounces of chicken breast provide around 44 grams.

If a plant-based meal is aiming for 30 grams of protein, tofu may need support from edamame, beans, grains, seeds or another source. The same serving of chicken already clears that target easily.

That does not make tofu a weak protein food. It means portion planning matters more when protein is less concentrated. A stir-fry with tofu, edamame and a grain can distribute protein across several foods instead of relying on one ingredient to do all of the work.

More fat in tofu does not mean worse fat

Most of tofu's fat comes from soybeans and is largely unsaturated. Skinless chicken breast contains much less total fat.

That contrast explains why the two foods can be relatively close in calories even though chicken has almost twice the protein per 100 grams.

If lowering total fat is the main goal, lean chicken starts with an advantage. If the goal is building a plant-based meal with unsaturated fat, tofu's fat is part of its normal food profile rather than a flaw that has to be eliminated.

Tofu calcium can vary dramatically by brand

When calcium sulfate is used as the coagulant, a serving of tofu can provide several hundred milligrams of calcium. Tofu made with another coagulant may contain far less.

So it is not useful to memorize one calcium number for “tofu.” In this case, the label can genuinely change the comparison.

Water content matters too. Extra-firm tofu can concentrate more protein per 100 grams than a softer product, while sodium and calcium can differ among brands. Two packages both labeled tofu may therefore produce noticeably different numbers.

Chicken provides B12 naturally; tofu does not

Chicken breast contributes vitamin B12, niacin, vitamin B6 and selenium. Tofu provides nonheme iron, some magnesium, fiber and soy compounds, but it is not a reliable natural source of B12 unless fortified.

On a vegan diet, eating more tofu does not solve the B12 question by itself. B12 needs a reliable source such as fortified foods or supplementation according to the individual's dietary plan. In an omnivorous diet, chicken can contribute B12 alongside other animal foods.

Less protein does not mean incomplete protein

Soy supplies all nine essential amino acids in favorable proportions and has good digestibility. The main difference from chicken is the amount of protein per unit weight, not that tofu is “missing” essential amino acids.

Protein quality and protein density are different ideas. A food can have a strong amino-acid pattern while still supplying fewer total grams of protein because it contains more water, fat or other components.

Cooking method can matter more than the base food

Breaded fried tofu can absorb a lot of oil; breaded fried chicken can too. If one is fried and the other grilled, the basic-food comparison no longer represents the final dishes fairly.

Sauces matter as well. A salty glaze can make tofu much higher in sodium than the plain product, while butter, cheese or breading can push chicken calories and fat upward. For a real meal, compare the full preparation rather than the naked ingredients alone.

What to remember

Tofu and chicken can fill the same culinary role without having the same nutrition profile. Chicken concentrates far more protein; tofu combines plant protein with unsaturated fat, some fiber and, depending on the product, substantial calcium. The swap can work very well, but serving size and the rest of the meal may need adjusting if you are targeting a specific amount of protein.

faq.question: Which has more protein, tofu or chicken?
faq.answer: Cooked chicken breast has about 31 g/100 g versus roughly 15–18 g/100 g in firm tofu.

faq.question: Is tofu a complete protein?
faq.answer: Yes. Soy provides all nine essential amino acids in favorable proportions.

faq.question: Does tofu contain calcium?
faq.answer: It can contain a lot when set with calcium sulfate; other tofus contain much less, so check the label.
